title: Enterprise Wireless: 802.11, Lightweight APs, WLCs and WLAN Security
intro: Enterprise wireless is an 802.11 radio network that connects client devices to the wired network through access points (APs), usually managed centrally by a Wireless LAN Controller (WLC). This lesson teaches the 802.11 connection process, the lightweight AP and CAPWAP architecture, core WLC concepts, WLAN security from WEP to WPA3, the wireless attacks an analyst must recognize, and how to read wireless telemetry while troubleshooting a failed connection.

sections.heading: 802.11 fundamentals: names, bands and channels
sections.content:
802.11 is the IEEE family of standards that defines the radio link between a client (a station, or STA) and an access point. It covers Layers 1 and 2 only. VLAN tagging and IP addressing on the wired side are covered in the existing networking lessons and are not repeated here. Think of an AP as a hub in the air: every device in range on the same channel hears the same conversation, so the medium is shared.

Three names are constantly confused, and the confusion causes real investigative mistakes.

| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| SSID | Human-readable network name, up to 32 bytes, carried in beacons and probes | CORP-WIFI |
| BSSID | MAC address of one AP radio for one SSID; identifies one BSS | 4c:77:6d:1a:02:b1 |
| BSS | One AP radio plus the clients associated to it | AP-B2-F3-014 on 5 GHz |
| ESS | Several BSSs sharing one SSID, joined by the wired network, so clients can roam | every AP that broadcasts CORP-WIFI |

One radio can broadcast several SSIDs, each with its own BSSID (usually the base MAC with the last bits incremented). The 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz radios of the same AP also have different BSSIDs. Pitfall: if you correlate only by SSID you will merge a legitimate AP with an attacker AP that copies the name. The BSSID, and the OUI (vendor prefix) inside it, is what identifies the physical radio. A hidden SSID is not a secret either: the name still appears in probe requests and association frames, so any sniffer reads it.

**Bands and channels**

| Band | Spectrum | Typical widths | What to remember |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.4 GHz | 2.400 to 2.4835 GHz | 20 MHz | Only 3 non-overlapping channels in the US (1, 6, 11); best range, most interference (Bluetooth, microwave ovens, neighbours) |
| 5 GHz | about 5.15 to 5.85 GHz | 20, 40, 80, 160 MHz | Many non-overlapping channels; DFS channels (roughly 52 to 144) must vacate when radar is detected |
| 6 GHz | 5.925 to 7.125 GHz | 20 to 320 MHz | Wi-Fi 6E and 7 only; no legacy devices; WPA3 (or OWE) is mandatory |

Generations map to bands: 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) runs on 2.4 and 5, 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) on 5 only, 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6, and 6E with the 6 GHz band) and 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7) on all three. Higher frequency means shorter range and weaker wall penetration, which is why a laptop that sees the SSID at the edge of a floor may be hearing only the 2.4 GHz radio. Channel width is a trade: a wider channel gives more throughput but leaves fewer non-overlapping channels, so dense deployments use 20 or 40 MHz.

**What to ask:** Which band and channel was the client on? Is the BSSID in the AP inventory? Does the client hardware even support that band?

sections.heading: Half-duplex access and the connection steps
sections.content:
Wireless is half-duplex: a radio cannot transmit and listen on the same channel at the same moment, so it cannot detect a collision the way old wired Ethernet did. Instead 802.11 uses CSMA/CA (carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance). A station listens first, waits a random backoff when the medium is busy, transmits, and expects an ACK for every unicast frame. No ACK means the sender assumes a collision and retries, setting the retry bit in the next frame. Optional RTS/CTS lets a station reserve the air, which helps with the hidden node problem (two clients that hear the AP but not each other).

Practical consequences for an analyst: airtime is the scarce resource, not bandwidth. One client stuck at a low legacy rate occupies the channel longer than a fast one and slows everybody. A high retry percentage in AP statistics means interference or poor signal. Management frames (beacon, probe, authentication, association, deauthentication, disassociation) are unencrypted by default, which is the root of several attacks covered later. Protected Management Frames (PMF, 802.11w) fix this for unicast management traffic.

**The connection sequence**

```
1. Scan
   passive: listen for beacons (about every 102.4 ms)
   active : send Probe Request, AP answers Probe Response
2. 802.11 authentication (Open System, 2 frames, no real security)
   with WPA3-SAE the same frames carry SAE commit and confirm
3. Association
   request: supported rates, capabilities, RSN information element
   response: status code 0 = success, plus an Association ID (AID)
4. Security exchange
   Enterprise: 802.1X / EAP exchange with RADIUS
   then the 4-way handshake installs the encryption keys
5. Controlled port opens, client sends DHCP, gets an IP in the WLAN's VLAN
```

Terminology pitfall: the 802.11 'authentication' in step 2 proves nothing about identity. Real authentication happens in step 4 (EAP, or knowledge of the PSK proven in the handshake). A client can therefore be 'associated' and still have no network access.

Useful codes that show up in logs and captures:

| Code | Meaning | Typical cause |
|---|---|---|
| Status 0 | Success | Normal association |
| Status 17 | AP cannot handle more stations | AP or radio at client limit |
| Reason 15 | 4-way handshake timeout | Wrong PSK, or lost handshake frames |
| Reason 23 | 802.1X authentication failed | RADIUS reject or timeout |
| Reason 7 | Class 3 frame from non-associated station | Often spoofed deauth or stale state |
| Reason 3 | Station is leaving | Normal disconnect |

**What to ask:** At which step did the client stop? Scan (no SSID visible), association (rejected), security (handshake or EAP), or IP (DHCP)? The step tells you which team and which log to look at.

sections.heading: Autonomous APs, lightweight APs and CAPWAP
sections.content:
An autonomous AP is a complete device: it carries its own configuration, runs its own security and bridges clients straight onto the wired VLAN. With ten APs you configure ten devices. This does not scale, and policy drifts between devices.

The enterprise answer is the split-MAC architecture. A lightweight AP (LAP) keeps only the real-time work: transmitting beacons and probe responses, sending ACKs, encrypting and decrypting frames on the radio, and retransmissions. The Wireless LAN Controller takes the non-real-time work: client authentication and association management, security policy, WLAN-to-VLAN mapping, radio resource management (automatic channel and power), and roaming.

| Aspect | Autonomous AP | Lightweight AP + WLC |
|---|---|---|
| Configuration | Per device | Central on the controller |
| Radio tuning | Manual | Automatic (RRM) |
| Roaming | Weak, per device | Coordinated by the controller |
| Rogue detection | Limited | Built in, APs scan off-channel |
| Failure impact | One AP | Controller is a critical dependency |

**CAPWAP** (RFC 5415) is the protocol between the AP and the controller. It builds two tunnels, both over UDP:

| Tunnel | UDP port | Carries | Protection |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | 5246 | Join, configuration, monitoring, firmware | DTLS, always |
| Data | 5247 | Client traffic encapsulated to the WLC | DTLS optional |

AP join sequence: the AP gets an IP by DHCP, then discovers a controller (DHCP option 43, a DNS name, a broadcast, or a stored list), sends a Discovery Request, picks a controller from the responses, builds the DTLS control tunnel with its certificate, joins, downloads firmware if needed, and receives its configuration. Pitfalls when an AP will not join: no DHCP option 43 or DNS entry, a firewall blocking UDP 5246 or 5247, certificate validity problems caused by a wrong clock, a regulatory domain mismatch, or the controller AP license limit. CAPWAP adds header overhead, so MTU and fragmentation problems cause strange partial failures.

**AP modes**

| Mode | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Local | Default. All client data is tunneled to the WLC, which places it on the VLAN. AP switchport is an access port in the management VLAN |
| FlexConnect | Client data can be switched locally at the branch, so the site survives a WAN outage; switchport is a trunk |
| Monitor | No clients served; dedicated to scanning for rogues and attacks |
| Sniffer | Captures 802.11 frames and forwards them to an analyzer |

A consequence to remember: in local mode a client's traffic exits the network at the controller, not at the AP. The source switchport you see for wireless traffic is the WLC port.

sections.heading: WLC concepts: WLANs, VLAN mapping, AP groups and roaming
sections.content:
On the controller, a WLAN is a profile that binds together an SSID, a security method and a place to put the client traffic. The core idea is the WLAN-to-VLAN mapping: the WLAN decides which VLAN (through a controller interface) the clients land in. Vendors use different menus, but the content looks like this.

```
WLAN 10  profile CORP-WIFI   ssid CORP-WIFI
         security : WPA2 (AES) + 802.1X, RADIUS server 10.20.5.11
         vlan     : 110 (staff)
WLAN 20  profile GUEST-WIFI  ssid GUEST-WIFI
         security : open + web authentication
         vlan     : 920 (guest, isolated)
AP group BLDG-A-FLOOR2 : WLAN 10, WLAN 20
AP group BLDG-B-LAB    : WLAN 10 mapped to vlan 140
```

An AP group is a named set of APs that broadcast a chosen list of WLANs, and it can override the VLAN for a WLAN. This is how one SSID such as CORP-WIFI lands on a different VLAN and subnet in building B than in building A, or how a lab SSID is limited to specific APs. RF profiles attach per-group radio settings such as which bands are enabled and the minimum data rate. Two classic pitfalls: a VLAN that exists on the controller but is not allowed on the trunk toward the switch (clients associate and authenticate, then get no DHCP lease), and a RADIUS-assigned VLAN (Tunnel-Private-Group-ID) that silently overrides the WLAN default.

**Roaming at a concept level**

Roaming means a client moves between APs without dropping sessions. The client decides when to move; the network only helps.

| Type | Situation | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Intra-controller | Both APs joined to the same WLC | The controller just updates which AP serves the client; IP stays the same |
| Inter-controller, Layer 2 | Different WLCs, same VLAN and subnet on both | Client entry moves to the new controller within a mobility group |
| Inter-controller, Layer 3 | Different WLCs, different subnets | Controllers tunnel the traffic back to the original (anchor) controller so the client keeps its IP |

A full 802.1X re-authentication on every roam takes hundreds of milliseconds and breaks voice calls. Fast-roaming features avoid it: PMK caching and opportunistic key caching reuse the earlier authentication, 802.11r (Fast Transition) pre-computes keys for the target AP, and 802.11k and 802.11v let the AP suggest candidate neighbors to the client. For an analyst, a burst of association events for one client MAC across many AP names in seconds is usually roaming, not an attack.

**What to ask:** Which WLAN and AP group did the client hit? Which VLAN was it placed in, by the WLAN default or by a RADIUS override?

sections.heading: Wireless security: from WEP to WPA3 and the 4-way handshake
sections.content:
Because radio waves cross walls, wireless security must protect confidentiality, not only access. The history is a list of broken designs, and an analyst should know why each is dead.

| Protocol | Cipher | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Open | None | Everything readable by anyone nearby; acceptable only for guest with other controls |
| WEP | RC4 with a 24-bit IV | Broken: IVs repeat, key recovered from tens of thousands of captured packets in minutes |
| WPA | RC4 with TKIP | Transitional, deprecated |
| WPA2 | AES-CCMP | Still widespread; secure if the key is strong |
| WPA3 | AES-GCMP, SAE for Personal | Current; PMF required |

| Feature | WPA2-Personal | WPA3-Personal |
|---|---|---|
| Key setup | PSK turned into a key with PBKDF2 | SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), a password-authenticated key exchange |
| Offline guessing from captured frames | Possible | Not possible; each guess needs a live exchange |
| Forward secrecy | No; a later-learned passphrase decrypts old captures | Yes |
| Management frame protection | Optional | Mandatory |
| Open networks | No protection | OWE (Enhanced Open) encrypts without a password |

Many networks run transition mode (WPA2 and WPA3 on one SSID), and a downgrade to WPA2 keeps WPA2 weaknesses in play.

**The 4-way handshake (high level)**

Both sides must end up with fresh, per-session keys without ever sending the secret. They start from a shared Pairwise Master Key (PMK). With a PSK, PMK = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1(passphrase, SSID, 4096 iterations, 256 bits), which is why the SSID name is part of the key derivation. With Enterprise, the PMK comes from the EAP exchange. With WPA3, SAE produces it.

```
Msg 1  AP  -> STA : ANonce (random number from the AP)
Msg 2  STA -> AP  : SNonce + MIC   (STA now computes the PTK)
       PTK = PRF(PMK, ANonce, SNonce, AP MAC, STA MAC)
Msg 3  AP  -> STA : MIC + encrypted GTK (group key for broadcast)
Msg 4  STA -> AP  : ACK, keys are installed, encryption starts
```

The MIC in message 2 proves the client knew the PMK. The password never crosses the air, yet the exchange leaks something useful to an attacker: with PSK, anyone who captures messages 1 and 2 can test passphrase guesses offline, because a correct guess reproduces the MIC. That single fact drives the attack section of this lesson, and also the reason WPA3 exists.

**What to ask:** Which security mode does the SSID use? Is PMF required? Is a transition mode keeping WPA2 alive?

sections.heading: WPA2-Personal versus WPA2-Enterprise: 802.1X, EAP and RADIUS
sections.content:
Personal mode shares one passphrase among everyone. Enterprise mode gives every user or device its own credentials through IEEE 802.1X.

| Aspect | Personal (PSK) | Enterprise (802.1X) |
|---|---|---|
| Credential | One shared passphrase | Per-user password or per-device certificate |
| Server needed | None | RADIUS server (plus a directory or CA) |
| Offboarding | Change the passphrase for everyone | Disable one account |
| Per-user keys | Derived from the shared PSK | Unique PMK per session |
| Attribution in logs | Only a client MAC | User name, MAC, AP, time |
| Typical use | Home, small office, guest, IoT | Corporate staff and managed devices |

**The three roles**

- Supplicant: the client software.
- Authenticator: the AP or WLC; it relays and enforces, it does not decide.
- Authentication server: the RADIUS server that decides.

The client and RADIUS talk using EAP (RFC 3748), a framework carried inside EAPOL over the air and inside RADIUS between the WLC and the server. The WLC and RADIUS server share a secret and speak UDP 1812 for authentication and 1813 for accounting. Change of Authorization (CoA) uses UDP 3799 and lets the server disconnect or re-policy a live session.

```
STA -> AP/WLC : EAPOL-Start
AP/WLC -> STA : EAP-Request/Identity
STA -> AP/WLC : EAP-Response/Identity  (jdoe@corp.example)
WLC -> RADIUS : Access-Request  (User-Name, Calling-Station-Id=client MAC,
                Called-Station-Id=BSSID:SSID, NAS-IP-Address)
   ... TLS tunnel is built, inner method runs ...
RADIUS -> WLC : Access-Accept   (PMK delivered, optional VLAN and ACL)
                or Access-Reject
STA <-> AP    : 4-way handshake, then DHCP
```

Common EAP methods:

| Method | Client proves identity by | Note |
|---|---|---|
| PEAP-MSCHAPv2 | Username and password inside a TLS tunnel | Most common; safe only if the client validates the server certificate |
| EAP-TLS | Client certificate and server certificate (mutual) | Strongest; needs a PKI |
| EAP-TTLS | Password inside a TLS tunnel | Similar to PEAP |

Pitfalls that matter to defenders: a client configured to 'not validate the server certificate' will hand its MSCHAPv2 exchange to an evil twin; a shared secret mismatch between WLC and RADIUS makes the server discard requests without any user-visible reason; and the RADIUS-returned Tunnel-Private-Group-ID can place users in a VLAN different from the WLAN default. Because RADIUS carries the authentication outcome and the user name, its logs are the best attribution source you have for wireless.

**What to ask:** Which EAP method is in use? Does the client check the server certificate? Which RADIUS server answered, and what reason did it give for a reject?

sections.heading: Wireless attacks an analyst should recognize
sections.content:
Wireless attacks live in the radio layer, so many never touch a firewall. The defender's view comes from the controller, from monitor-mode APs, and from correlating with wired-side data. For general credential and handshake concepts see the existing credential lessons; here the focus is on how each attack appears.

| Attack | What the attacker does | What you observe |
|---|---|---|
| Rogue AP | Connects an unauthorized AP (often a cheap consumer router) to a wall jack, bypassing the secured wireless design | Unknown BSSID reported by APs; the same device's MAC seen on a wired switchport; OUI of a consumer vendor |
| Evil twin | Broadcasts a copy of a real SSID with stronger signal; clients join it; attacker relays or harvests credentials | Known SSID from a BSSID not in the inventory, on an odd channel, with different capabilities; clients suddenly associating to it |
| Deauthentication / disassociation | Sends spoofed management frames that appear to come from the AP, so clients drop | Bursts of deauth or disassoc events, reason codes 1, 3 or 7, many clients at once |
| PSK handshake capture and cracking | Captures messages 1 and 2 (or a PMKID) and guesses the passphrase offline | Often only a preceding deauth burst and an immediate client reconnect; the cracking itself leaves no network trace |

**How they chain.** A common sequence is deauth followed by a client reconnecting. The attacker can use that reconnect to capture the handshake, or to steer the client toward an evil twin that wins on signal strength. Against Enterprise, an evil twin with a fake RADIUS server aims to capture PEAP-MSCHAPv2 exchanges from clients that do not validate the server certificate.

**Detection ideas**

- Compare every BSSID seen in scanning against the managed AP inventory; an SSID match with an unknown BSSID is the evil twin signature.
- Correlate rogue radio MACs with the wired CAM table to separate a neighbour's AP (nuisance) from a device plugged into your network (incident).
- Alert on deauth rates above a baseline rather than single frames, since normal roaming creates a few.
- A cracked PSK is invisible. If you have a PSK SSID, treat a deauth-then-reconnect pattern as a reason to rotate the key, not just to log it.

**Mitigations to recommend:** require PMF; use WPA3 or Enterprise with EAP-TLS; enforce server certificate validation on managed clients; use a long random PSK of 20 or more characters if a PSK is unavoidable; keep monitor-mode APs or a WIPS enabled; use controller rogue containment only after legal and operational review, since it sends deauths of its own.

**What to ask:** Is the BSSID known? Is the radio also on the wired network? Who is affected, and which credential could have been exposed?

sections.heading: Where wireless appears in logs and telemetry
sections.content:
No single log tells the whole wireless story. You combine several sources, and the join keys are the client MAC, the BSSID and the user name.

| Source | Key fields | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| WLC syslog and events | Client MAC, AP name, BSSID, SSID, band, channel, RSSI, VLAN, reason code | Where and when did the client associate, roam or fail? |
| RADIUS / AAA logs | User-Name, Calling-Station-Id, Called-Station-Id, NAS-Identifier, EAP type, result and reason | Who authenticated, with what method, and why was it rejected? |
| DHCP server | Client MAC, lease IP, hostname | Did the client get an address, and in which scope? |
| Wireless IDS or rogue reports | Unknown BSSID, SSID, channel, detecting AP, classification | Is there a rogue AP, evil twin or deauth flood? |
| Switch tables | MAC on a port, VLAN | Is a rogue also on the wired network? |

Illustrative controller events for one failed enterprise login:

```
Nov  2 08:41:07 wlc01 assoc    client=a4:83:e7:5c:19:2d ap=AP-B2-F3-014 bssid=4c:77:6d:1a:02:b1 ssid=CORP-WIFI band=5GHz ch=44 rssi=-61
Nov  2 08:41:07 wlc01 dot1x    client=a4:83:e7:5c:19:2d state=EAP-identity user=jdoe
Nov  2 08:41:09 wlc01 radius   server=10.20.5.11 Access-Request retry 1 of 3, no response
Nov  2 08:41:15 wlc01 radius   server=10.20.5.11 timeout, authentication failed
Nov  2 08:41:15 wlc01 deauth   client=a4:83:e7:5c:19:2d reason=23
```

On a Windows network policy server the matching entry for a rejected login is event 6273, with fields such as Account Name, Calling Station Identifier (client MAC), Called Station Identifier (AP BSSID and SSID), NAS Port Type 'Wireless - IEEE 802.11', Authentication Type (for example PEAP) and a Reason Code. Reason Code 16 means the credentials did not match. A successful login is event 6272.

**Analyst pitfalls**

- MAC randomization: modern phones and laptops use a different private MAC per SSID, so the MAC in the WLC may not match the one in an inventory. Pivot through the RADIUS user name and the DHCP hostname.
- Roaming noise: many association events across AP names in short time are normal; judge by reason codes and failures, not raw counts.
- Clock skew between WLC, RADIUS and DHCP breaks timelines; check time sources first.
- Sampling gaps: a deauth flood seen by one monitor AP may not appear in client-side logs at all.

**What to ask:** Do the WLC and RADIUS records agree on the same client and time? Which step in the connection sequence is the last one logged? Which key (MAC, BSSID, user) can I pivot on?

sections.heading: Worked example: a client cannot get on the corporate WLAN
sections.content:
Ticket: 'New laptop shows CORP-WIFI but will not connect. Other staff are fine.' Work down the connection sequence and stop at the first step that fails. The goal is to find the layer, not to guess.

**Step 1: Does the client see the SSID, and on which band?** Check whether the laptop is 2.4 GHz only or lacks 6 GHz support, and whether the WLAN is enabled on that band for this AP group via its RF profile. A WLAN limited to 5 GHz is invisible to an old 2.4 GHz adapter. Confirm the SSID spelling; a saved profile with a typo or an old security type fails silently.

**Step 2: Does association succeed?** Look for the client MAC in the WLC. No record means the client never reached an AP (range, band, or a wrong profile). An association with status 17 means an AP at its client limit.

**Step 3: PSK or 802.1X?** The security type decides what to check next.

| Symptom in logs | Likely cause | Next check |
|---|---|---|
| Reason 15, handshake timeout, on a PSK SSID | Wrong passphrase, or a WPA3-only client on a WPA2 SSID | Re-enter the key; compare security type |
| EAP started, client stops, no RADIUS entry | Client lacks a certificate, or does not trust the server certificate | Check the supplicant profile and certificate store |
| WLC shows Access-Request retries, server silent | RADIUS unreachable or shared secret mismatch | Ping and port test from the WLC, compare the secret |
| RADIUS event 6273 with Reason Code 16 | Bad username or password | Check the account state and password |
| Access-Accept, but no IP | Wrong VLAN, VLAN not on trunk, or DHCP scope issue | See the next step |

**Step 4: RADIUS reachable?** From the WLC management interface confirm that UDP 1812 and 1813 are permitted by any firewall, that the WLC is registered as a RADIUS client with the right shared secret, and that the server is up. A mismatched secret produces discarded requests, so the WLC sees only timeouts, and the user sees 'cannot connect'.

**Step 5: Authenticated but no address?** Confirm which VLAN the client was placed in: the WLAN default or a RADIUS-assigned one. Then check that this VLAN exists on the controller, is allowed on the trunk to the switch (or to the AP port in FlexConnect), and has a working DHCP scope. The switching and addressing details are covered in the existing VLAN and IP lessons.

**Resolution in this case:** the controller log showed Access-Request retries to 10.20.5.11 and reason 23. A firewall change the previous night had blocked UDP 1812 from the new WLC management subnet. Other users were already connected with cached sessions and did not exercise the path. Opening the port fixed the login, and the ticket was closed with a note to add a RADIUS reachability alert.

**Habit to keep:** always name the last successful step from the log, and the first failing one. That sentence is the heart of a good escalation.

quiz.question: Which statement about CAPWAP between a lightweight AP and its controller is correct?

options.label: Control and data share UDP 5246, and client traffic never leaves the AP switchport
Control uses UDP 5246 under DTLS, and local-mode client data uses UDP 5247
Control runs over TCP 443 with mutual TLS, and data runs over UDP 5247 in clear
Control uses UDP 1812 and data uses UDP 1813, borrowed from the RADIUS ports

quiz.explanation: CAPWAP builds a DTLS-protected control tunnel on UDP 5246 for join, configuration and monitoring, and a separate data tunnel on UDP 5247 that carries encapsulated client traffic in local mode. The claim that both tunnels share one port and traffic stays at the AP is wrong, because in local mode client data is tunneled to the controller. The TCP 443 description is wrong because CAPWAP is UDP-only and its data tunnel can also be DTLS-protected. UDP 1812 and 1813 belong to RADIUS authentication and accounting between the controller and the authentication server, not to the AP tunnels.

quiz.question: A new laptop associates to a WPA2-Enterprise SSID, then drops after about ten seconds with reason 23. The controller log shows repeated Access-Request retries to the RADIUS server, while a PSK guest SSID works for everyone. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The channel is badly overloaded, so data frames keep colliding and failing
The WLAN-to-VLAN mapping points at a VLAN that is missing from the trunk
The laptop only supports 2.4 GHz while the SSID is broadcast on 5 GHz
The WLC cannot reach the RADIUS server, or its shared secret mismatches

quiz.explanation: Retries of Access-Request with no answer, followed by an 802.1X failure, point to the controller-to-RADIUS path: a blocked port, a down server, or a shared secret that makes the server discard requests. A missing VLAN on the trunk would show up only after successful authentication, as a client with no DHCP lease. A band mismatch would mean the laptop never sees the SSID or never associates, but here the association and EAP start were logged. Channel overload slows traffic and raises retries on data frames, but it does not generate RADIUS timeouts while the guest SSID on the same radios works.

quiz.question: On a WPA2-Personal SSID without PMF, an analyst sees a burst of deauthentication frames spoofed from the AP BSSID aimed at one client, followed by that client reassociating within seconds. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: A forced reconnect meant to capture the 4-way handshake for offline guessing
Ordinary 802.11r roaming, where the client leaves one AP for a better one
A RADIUS timeout, which makes the controller expel the client repeatedly
A DFS radar event, which forces every client on the channel to move away

quiz.explanation: Spoofed deauth frames aimed at a single client, followed by a quick reconnect on a PSK network lacking management frame protection, is the classic way to make a client repeat the 4-way handshake so an attacker can record it and test passphrase guesses offline. Normal roaming does not involve unsolicited deauth frames that appear to come from the AP itself. A RADIUS timeout is irrelevant because a Personal SSID has no RADIUS exchange. A DFS radar event moves the whole channel and affects all clients through a channel switch announcement, not a targeted deauth to one device.

quiz.question: Why is a captured exchange less useful against WPA3-Personal than against WPA2-Personal?

options.label: It encrypts the beacon and probe frames, so there is no handshake left to capture
It swaps the passphrase for per-device certificates issued by the controller
SAE needs a live exchange per guess, so captured frames cannot be tested offline
It raises PBKDF2 to millions of iterations so every offline guess takes minutes

quiz.explanation: SAE is a password-authenticated key exchange, so an attacker must interact with the AP or client for every passphrase guess, and recorded traffic does not reveal material that can be checked offline. It also gives forward secrecy. Beacons and probes remain unencrypted in WPA3 because clients must find networks before any keys exist. WPA3-Personal still uses a shared password, not certificates, which belong to Enterprise with EAP-TLS. Increasing PBKDF2 iterations would only slow cracking down, while WPA3 removes the offline attack path altogether.

quiz.question: A client roams to an AP joined to a different controller, and the WLAN maps to a different subnet there. How is the client allowed to keep its IP address and sessions?

options.label: The client sends a fresh DHCP request, so the IP address changes on every such roam
The controllers form a mobility tunnel and anchor the client on the original WLC
The new AP bridges the client frames to the old subnet over a shared VLAN trunk
The old AP keeps serving the client and relays the radio signal to the new AP

quiz.explanation: In a Layer 3 inter-controller roam, the controllers in a mobility group set up a tunnel and the original controller stays the anchor, so the client keeps its address and the foreign controller forwards its traffic through the tunnel. Requesting a new lease would break open sessions, which is exactly what the feature avoids. Bridging directly onto the old subnet is not how the roam works, because the new controller's VLAN is in a different subnet and the point is not to extend VLANs. APs do not relay each other's radio signals; each AP serves only the clients associated to its own radio.
